Yeah, so I think that's actually one of the more underappreciated pieces of the system. The basic observation is that no single frontier model is uniformly best across an entire evolutionary run. Some models are great at making bold, exploratory rewrites early on. Others are better at the careful, incremental refinements you need later, when you're squeezing out the last bits of performance. And which is which also depends heavily on the task.

So instead of hard-coding a model or picking a static mixture, we treat model selection as a multi-armed bandit. Each LLM is an arm. After a model proposes a mutation and we evaluate the resulting program, we look at how much it improved over its parent, the relative fitness gain, and use that as the reward signal. UCB then balances exploiting the model that's been most productive recently against exploring the others, since their usefulness might shift.

What's really interesting is watching the allocation change over the course of a run. You often see a phase where one model dominates because it keeps finding good improvements, and then, as the search moves into a different regime, the bandit naturally shifts budget toward a different model. It adapts to the non-stationarity of the search itself. That's something you'd be hard-pressed to design by hand.

It also ties into the broader theme of sample efficiency. Every LLM call and every evaluation costs something, so if you can route queries to whichever model is currently most likely to produce a useful mutation, you get to good solutions with far fewer generations.

That said, I don't think it's the final answer. The reward design matters a lot. Rewarding raw improvement can bias you toward models that make safe, small edits, and you might undervalue a model whose proposals rarely win immediately but open up new regions of the search space. So there's a lot of room to think about richer credit assignment, maybe rewarding novelty or downstream contributions, not just immediate fitness gains. But as a simple, robust starting point, the UCB approach has worked surprisingly well for us.

r002.rationale: The response says different models excel at different stages and describes the bandit shifting budget as the search enters a different regime.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really interesting, and it actually came out of a fairly pragmatic observation when we were building the AI Scientist and then later working on ShinkaEvolve. When you're doing evolutionary program search, you have this loop where an LLM proposes a mutation or a crossover of existing programs in your archive, you evaluate it, and you decide what goes back into the population. And the question is: which model do you ask? Because they're not all the same. Some models are great at making small, careful, incremental edits. Some models are much more willing to propose radical restructurings of the code. And crucially, what you want changes over the course of the search.

Early on, when you're in a fairly unexplored part of the search space, the bold, diverse proposals are often what you want, because the fitness landscape is rough and you just need to find promising basins. Later, when you've converged on a good family of solutions, you want models that refine, that don't break things, that make the one-line change that squeezes out another couple of percent. So a fixed allocation, like "always use model X" or "sample uniformly," is leaving a lot on the table.

So the natural framing is a bandit problem. Each LLM is an arm. The reward is some notion of improvement, we normalize the fitness gain of the child relative to the parent, so a model gets credit when it actually moves the needle rather than just when it produces a valid program. And then UCB gives you exactly the behavior you want: an exploration bonus that keeps you occasionally pulling the arms you haven't tried much, combined with an exploitation term that shifts budget toward whatever is currently working. And because the statistics are running estimates, the allocation adapts as the search progresses. You can actually watch it happen in the logs. A model that dominated the first few hundred generations gets its share eroded as the task shifts from exploration to refinement, and a different model takes over.

I'd be honest that it's not a perfect bandit in the textbook sense. The reward distribution is non-stationary by construction, because the population itself is changing underneath you, so the assumptions behind the regret guarantees don't really hold. We've looked at things like sliding windows and discounting to handle that. But empirically it's been one of those components where the ablation is quite clear: you get better sample efficiency than any single model alone, and you get it essentially for free in terms of compute, because the bookkeeping is trivial compared to an LLM call and a program evaluation.

The thing I like philosophically is that it treats the models as part of the evolutionary system rather than as a fixed oracle. The models are operators, and you're doing a sort of meta-level adaptation of your operator probabilities, which has a long history in evolutionary computation. We're just doing it with language models as the mutation operators, and I think that connects a lot of older ideas in the field to what people are doing now with LLM-driven discovery.

r002.rationale: The response says model preferences change as the search moves from exploration to refinement, describing one model losing share and another taking over.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as an adaptive allocation problem. As the evolutionary search progresses, the kinds of improvements you need can change, so you don’t necessarily want to commit to one language model for the entire run. A UCB-based approach gives you a way to balance exploiting models that have produced useful candidates with exploring models whose usefulness you’re still uncertain about.

The interesting complication is that the reward is nonstationary. A model that was productive early on might become less useful once the population has improved or moved into a different part of the search space. So I’d view the selection mechanism as a way to adapt the search, but not as a guarantee that we’re always picking the best model. How you define improvement, account for cost, and weigh recent performance matters a lot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as an exploration–exploitation problem within the search itself. You have a portfolio of language models, and you don’t necessarily know beforehand which one will produce useful mutations for a particular problem or stage of evolution. A UCB-based approach lets you learn that allocation online: you favor models that have been productive, while still trying models whose potential is uncertain.

What’s interesting is that usefulness can change as the population improves. A model that helps you make progress early on might not be the best choice for refining a very strong program. So I’d view this as an adaptive resource-allocation mechanism, rather than a way of identifying one universally best model. The important questions are how you define the reward, how you account for inference cost, and how quickly the selector responds when the search changes.
